title: How do hotels make money, and what matters in a hotel case?
description: Hotel economics for case interviews: occupancy, average daily rate, RevPAR, fixed costs, franchising and online travel agents, with a worked RevPAR example.
hook: Hotels, like airlines, sell a perishable product: an empty room tonight can never be sold again. That makes occupancy and pricing the heart of nearly every hotel case.
body:
The measures that matter

  • Occupancy: the share of rooms sold.
  • Average daily rate (ADR): average price per sold room.
  • RevPAR (revenue per available room) = occupancy × ADR. It captures both.

A worked example: price versus occupancy

Hotel A: 80% occupancy at £150 → RevPAR £120. Hotel B: 70% at £180 → RevPAR £126. Hotel B earns more per room despite being emptier. Before cutting prices to fill rooms, check what it does to RevPAR.

Who owns what

Many big hotel brands do not own most of their hotels. They franchise or manage them for owners, earning fees with far less capital. Online travel agents bring bookings but take commissions, so brands push direct booking.

Typical hotel case questions

  • Why has RevPAR fallen?
  • Should a luxury group launch a budget brand?
  • How can we reduce reliance on online travel agents?
  • Should we buy or franchise new hotels?

Understand why higher prices can lower room revenue

A 200-room hotel charges an average daily rate (ADR) of £150 and fills 80% of its rooms. Its room revenue per available room (RevPAR) is £150 × 80% = £120. Over a 365-day year, that implies 200 × 365 × £120 = £8.76 million of room revenue before food, meetings or other services. Room revenue is not profit; housekeeping, payroll, commissions, rent and building costs remain.

Suppose management raises ADR to £170, but occupancy slips to 65%. RevPAR falls to £110.50, even though the room price is higher. The relevant question is whether the extra revenue per occupied room compensates for lost occupancy and variable costs. A successful strategy might deliberately accept lower room revenue if it improves total profit or protects capacity for higher-value guests; check contribution, not only RevPAR.

Hotel owners, management companies and brands can be separate businesses. A branded hotel may pay franchise or management fees, while an owner bears most property investment. Online travel agencies add another layer: commission can make two apparently identical £150 bookings generate different net revenue.

For an interview, segment weekday and weekend demand, business and leisure travellers, direct and third-party bookings, and peak and off-peak seasons. If the hotel is underperforming, ask whether the issue is occupancy, realised rate, channel mix or operating cost before launching a discount.
